results.title: ‘She inspired my proposal’: Readers on Yayoi Kusama | Yayoi Kusama | The Guardian
results.content:
I have always loved Yayoi Kusama’s work, and when I visited an exhibition of hers on a gap year in Sydney I was spellbound by her infinity mirror rooms. I immediately thought, despite being single at the time, this is a fantastic space to propose in. Fast forward around eight years and I am on one knee holding a ring out to my partner inside an infinity mirror room in Helsinki, with excited and expectant Finns looking on. He said yes. At the wedding, the breakfast was held under polka dotted [...] Two years ago, while researching in Porto, I was encouraged by a friend to go see the Kusama retrospective at the museum in Parque de Serralves. I was fortunate to experience her remarkable installation Dots Obsession – Aspiring to Heaven’s Love. The powerful effect she termed as self-obliteration viscerally connected with me in that room. I didn’t exist, as I dissolved, the dots were everywhere. Humanity is blessed for her work and I’m grateful and humbled to have experienced it. David, [...] I only recently became aware of her work from a visit to Naoshima, Japan’s art island, where two of her pumpkins are on display. Red Pumpkin is particularly great as you can climb inside. On returning home I was surprised and delighted that a pumpkin sculpture had arrived at Goodwood Art Foundation in Sussex. I’m now researching where to find more pumpkins as they always make me smile. Sandie, 61, London

results.title: The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth | Art | The Guardian
results.content: It should not work. It should not even exist. Nothing about the Bayeux tapestry makes sense according to any norms of art: its creators couldn’t do proper portraits or pictorial depth or landscapes or any of the sophisticated things we associate with timeless masterpieces. When they depict a church, they have to write what it is: Ecclesia. But these artists – or who knows, perhaps she was a single artist – created something so stupefying and delightful, so abundant in visual thrills, horrors [...] thrills, horrors and humour, it beats almost everything else ever painted or carved – let alone embroidered on a strip of linen. [...] It’s that honesty that makes this not just a fascinating medieval relic but a universal depiction of the madness that is war. If the violence is stunningly real, so are its consequences. The dead bodies pile up in mounds as Saxon after Saxon falls. King Harold didn’t really get killed by an arrow in his eye we are told, but seeing the tapestry so close, it sure looks like it. Anyway, his royal body just joins the rest. In the final scenes, the peasants, the churls, get their revenge. Little

results.title: ‘My work has always been serious’: Maurizio Cattelan on his $6m banana, his gold toilet – and bringing Hitler and a pope to Berlin | Maurizio Cattelan | The Guardian
results.content:
Each major exhibition sends him on a rollercoaster of exhilaration and panic, he says, admitting to being “extremely desperate” while planning Night. “Do I suffer? Yes, I don’t like it. It’s always a challenge. I still need the rush. It’s a contradiction, but I love the hate of making a show. It’s a fix. It’s a dependency. Maybe a therapist would say, ‘We can solve your addiction problem.’ And I’d say, ‘No, no, I love it.’” [...] the exhibition.” Botti describes Cattelan’s work as “comic existentialism”, saying: “You laugh about something, but then the laugh gets stuck in your throat.” [...] However, now being in his 60s, he says: “Maybe I should think about who I want to pass my problems to. I’m super lucky. I did have doubts [as an artist]. But I jumped into the void and said, ‘If we overcome fear, there will be a fantastic dawn. A fantastic dawn.’”

results.content:
## ‘We just went for it’: five of Temi Adegbayibi’s best shots

Ayo Salawu (main picture)“This was the main image in my Royal Albert Hall exhibition. I’m always trying to figure out how to capture the energy of a drum solo in a still image; I’d been researching slow shutters, layering and double exposures. We shot it in a blackout studio in Greenwich, set up the drums, ordered some pizza and just went for it.”

Photograph: Temi Adegbayibi [...] His interest in movement has also become a technical fascination. Inspired by visual artist Kat Anderson, he began experimenting with slow shutter speeds, light and layering to create photographs that “almost feel like you’re painting with light”.
